adults.title: Closer to Him, Closer to Each Other
adults.big_idea: Jesus Christ has the power to unite us: the closer we come to Him, the closer we come to each other, and our covenants make us one people.
adults.objective: Learners will explain what truly unites us in the Savior’s Church and choose one small step toward Christ-centered unity with a specific person or group this week.
prepare: Read President Uchtdorf’s talk, “Christ-Centered Unity,” marking the paragraphs under “The Unity Jesus Christ Offers” and “The Unifying Power of the Sacrament.”
Bring a board and marker, or one large sheet of paper.
Bring a slip of paper and a pencil for each learner.
Write the three references for segment 3 on the board before class: Matthew 8:2–3; Matthew 8:5–10; Luke 10:30–37.

segments.name: What brings people together?
steps: After the opening prayer, ask the class to call out things that bring people together. List them quickly on the board: teams, causes, heritage, hobbies, work.

Explain that President Uchtdorf named several of these, even a favorite soccer team or brand of soft drink, and then taught what unites us in the Savior’s Church. Read the first key quote aloud (“In the Savior’s Church…”).
Ask the first question below and take two or three brief answers. Write the lesson’s question on the board: How does coming closer to Jesus Christ bring us closer to each other?
questions: When have you felt one with people you had little else in common with, because of the Savior?

segments.name: One by one, and together
steps: Explain that President Uchtdorf began with baptism. He taught that we enter the gate one by one, and yet baptism is also a unifying ordinance. Read the second key quote (“Through baptism…”).
Invite learners to read Mosiah 18:8–9 in pairs and mark every promise that involves another person.
Ask pairs to share one phrase they marked and what it has looked like in real life: a meal no one asked for, a ride, a quiet seat beside someone at a funeral.
Ask the questions below. Let several people answer before you add anything.
questions: President Uchtdorf said that at baptism we show we do not want to live only for ourselves. Where is that hardest for you right now?
Who has borne a burden with you? What did it teach you about being a covenant people?

segments.name: The Savior crosses every wall
steps: Summarize: the world Jesus Christ was born into was divided culturally, politically and religiously, and President Uchtdorf said it was not so different from our world today.

Divide the class into three groups. Give each one passage: Matthew 8:2–3; Matthew 8:5–10; Luke 10:30–37. Each group has three minutes to answer: Whom did others avoid, and what did the Savior do or teach?
Hear one sentence from each group.

Draw a triangle on the board. Write the Savior’s name at the top point and place two marks at the bottom corners. Move each mark up its side and let the class see what happens to the distance between them. Read the third key quote (“Jesus Christ has the power…”).

Point out that President Uchtdorf also taught that Satan seeks to divide us by making our differences feel like impassable barriers. Read Elder Sinclair’s words from this conference: “a true disciple of Jesus Christ is quick to help and slow to judge.”
questions: President Uchtdorf said that when our attention is riveted on Christ, superficial things are hardly worth noticing. What superficial things most easily divide us?
What changes in how you see a person when you first remember how the Savior sees them?

segments.name: The sacrament: not addressed by name
steps: Ask learners to read Moroni 4:3 silently and look for whose names are spoken in the prayer and for whom the bread is blessed.
Share President Uchtdorf’s observation: the sacrament is the only ordinance we receive in which we are not addressed by name. We partake individually but also as a group.
Read the fourth key quote (“The sacrament is a weekly reminder…”). Then read his invitation: “let us not miss the unifying power of the sacrament.”
Ask the questions below. Allow a moment of silence before the first answer.
questions: How might next Sunday’s sacrament feel different if you looked around the room and thought of everyone there as renewing covenants beside you?
Who in our ward might be feeling alone during the sacrament, and what could we do about it?

segments.name: One step this week
steps: Read President Uchtdorf’s assurance that we may not achieve perfect unity in this life, yet “Every step we take toward unity matters, however small it may seem.”

Hand out the slips of paper. Give two minutes of silent writing: one name or one group, and one small step toward unity with them this week. Suggest the list he gave: “a little more patient, a little kinder, more forgiving, more helpful, more neighborly.”

Read his invitation: “Please, come and see, come and help, and come and belong.” Then share his promise in your own words: the more united in Christ we are, and the more we desire to build bridges instead of walls, the more our lives, families, communities and nations will experience God’s presence and blessings.
As a check for understanding, ask one or two learners to answer the question on the board in a single sentence. Bear your testimony of the Savior’s power to make us one.
Follow up next week: begin class by asking who took a step toward unity and what they noticed. Thank each person who shares.

key_quotes.text: In the Savior’s Church, it is not our political views, culture, or personal interests that unite us. It is our love for God and neighbor, God’s children.
Through baptism, we become not only covenant individuals but also part of a covenant people.
Jesus Christ has the power to change us—you and me—purify us, and unite us. The closer we come to Him, the closer we will come to each other—and the closer we will come to the unity He wants for us.
The sacrament is a weekly reminder, a sacred reminder, that we are not alone. We have the Savior, and we have each other.

scriptures.use: Read in pairs in segment 2; mark every promise that involves another person and share what one of them looks like in real life.
One of three small-group passages in segment 3 (with Matthew 8:2–3 and Matthew 8:5–10): whom did others avoid, and what did the Savior do or teach?
Read silently in segment 4; look for whose names are spoken and for whom the bread is blessed.
Optional close: read it together just before the promise in segment 5 and ask where learners have felt it fulfilled.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Sinclair
aligned_quotes.text: a true disciple of Jesus Christ is quick to help and slow to judge

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Kyungu
aligned_quotes.text: Let us use the language that uplifts, edifies, comforts, and brings people together.

invitations.text: let us not miss the unifying power of the sacrament
Please, come and see, come and help, and come and belong.
I invite you to join the Christ-centered unity we are trying to build.

takeaways: What unites us in the Savior’s Church is love for God and neighbor and our covenants with Jesus Christ.
The closer I come to the Savior, the closer I come to the people around me.
The sacrament reminds me each week that I am not alone: I have the Savior, and we have each other.
act: Take the one step you wrote on your slip toward the person or group you named, before next Sunday.
During the sacrament this Sunday, look around the room and silently thank Heavenly Father for the people renewing covenants beside you.
Sit by, greet, or message someone who may feel like an outsider in the ward, and learn something new about them.
When a conversation turns to what divides people, choose words that bring people together, as Elder Kyungu invited.
adapt: At home or with fewer than six people: skip the three groups and read Luke 10:30–37 together; then do the triangle on a sheet of paper on the table.
Large class: do segments 2 and 3 with the people seated nearby and take only one comment from each side of the room.
Only 15 minutes: teach segments 1, 4 and 5, and use the third key quote in place of segment 3.

youth.title: Bridges, Not Walls
youth.big_idea: Jesus Christ reaches across every boundary to unite Heavenly Father’s family, and the closer we come to Him, the closer we come to each other.
youth.objective: Youth will describe how the Savior treated people others shut out and commit to one specific bridge they will build this week at school, at home, online, or at church.
prepare: Bring a picture of the Savior and tape, or something to stand it on.
Ask youth to have their scriptures or the Gospel Library app open.
Bring a small card or slip of paper and a pencil for each person.
Write the three situations for segment 4 on the board, covered until you need them.

segments.name: Pick a side
steps: As soon as the prayer ends, have everyone stand. Call out four quick choices and have them move to one side of the room or the other: mornings or nights, mountains or beach, cats or dogs, and one favorite local team against its rival.

While they are still standing in two groups, point out how fast we sorted ourselves. President Uchtdorf said people unite around causes, heritage, hobbies, even a favorite soccer team, and often with very strong feelings.
Ask the question below, then have them sit anywhere except by the person they came in with.
questions: What could unite every person in this room, no matter which side you just stood on?

segments.name: Whom did Jesus reach?
steps: Explain that in the world Jesus Christ was born into, Jews and Samaritans avoided each other and Gentiles were considered unclean. President Uchtdorf said it wasn’t so different from our world today.

Put youth in pairs and give each pair one passage: Matthew 8:2–3; Matthew 8:5–10; or Luke 10:30–37. Friendly race: the first pair for each passage to stand and say who the outsider was and what the Savior did or taught earns the right to choose the closing song.
After the three reports, read the first key quote (“He consistently reached out…”).
questions: Who are the outsiders in the places you spend your days? You do not need to name anyone; describe the kind of person.
Why is it honestly hard to reach out to them?

segments.name: Closer to Him, closer to each other
steps: Ask someone to read 4 Nephi 1:15, 17 aloud while everyone else looks for what was missing among the people and what they were called.

Explain that President Uchtdorf described the Nephites and Lamanites as having one of the longest-running sibling rivalries in the world, and that everything changed when Jesus Christ appeared, taught His gospel and established His Church.

Demonstration: place the picture of the Savior at the front. Send two volunteers to opposite back corners. Each time the class names something that brings a person closer to Christ (prayer, repentance, the sacrament, serving, forgiving), both take a step toward the picture. Stop when they are shoulder to shoulder.
Ask the class what they saw. Then read the second key quote (“The closer we come to Him…”).
Be honest that President Uchtdorf also named the opposite pull: Satan seeks to divide us and isolate us from each other by making our differences feel like impassable barriers.
questions: Where do you see people being pushed apart or isolated right now?
Why would coming closer to the Savior change how two people feel about each other?

segments.name: What would a bridge look like?
steps: Read the third key quote (“When we try to be a little more patient…”). Say that President Uchtdorf’s picture of unity is made of small things like these.

Uncover the three situations and form three groups, one for each. (1) Someone new comes to an activity and stands alone by the door. (2) A group chat starts making fun of a person who is not in it. (3) Two friends in the same class or quorum disagree strongly and stop talking.

Give groups three minutes to plan a short role play, 30 seconds at most, that shows one realistic thing a disciple of Jesus Christ could say or do. Realistic means something they would actually do on a Tuesday.
Watch each role play. After each, ask the class what made it a bridge and not a wall.

Share two helps from this conference. President Chibota: “Often, helping others feel seen as children of God begins with something as simple as learning their name.” Elder Kyungu: “Let us use the language that uplifts, edifies, comforts, and brings people together.”
questions: Does being united mean we have to agree on everything or like all the same things? What did President Uchtdorf say unites us?

segments.name: The ordinance with no names
steps: Ask everyone to open Moroni 4:3 and find whose names are used in the prayer. Ask who helps with the sacrament and what they have noticed.
Share what President Uchtdorf pointed out: the sacrament is the only ordinance we receive in which we are not addressed by name. We partake individually but also as a group.
Read the fourth key quote (“We have the Savior, and we have each other.”) and his invitation: “let us not miss the unifying power of the sacrament.”
questions: What could you think about during the sacrament this Sunday that would help you feel part of a covenant people and not just an individual in a row?

segments.name: Build one bridge
steps: Hand out the cards. Give 90 seconds of silent writing: one person or group, one place (school, home, online, church), and one bridge they will build before next Sunday. It stays private.
Read President Uchtdorf’s invitation: “Please, come and see, come and help, and come and belong.” Add his words to anyone who wonders whether they are needed: “It would be incomplete without you.”

Share his promise in your own words: the more united in Christ we are and the more we desire to build bridges instead of walls, the more we, our families and our communities will experience God’s presence and blessings.
Check for understanding: ask each youth to finish this sentence aloud in a few words — What unites us is…
Follow up next week: start class by asking for bridge reports. Share your own first. Close with the song the winning pair chose and a prayer.

key_quotes.text: He consistently reached out to those who would otherwise be shunned as outsiders.
The closer we come to Him, the closer we will come to each other—and the closer we will come to the unity He wants for us.
When we try to be a little more patient, a little kinder, more forgiving, more helpful, more neighborly, there will be less room for pride or judgmental attitudes or contention.
We have the Savior, and we have each other.

scriptures.use: One of three pair passages in segment 2 (with Matthew 8:2–3 and Matthew 8:5–10): find the outsider and what the Savior did or taught.
Read aloud in segment 3; look for what was missing among the people and what they were called.
Open in segment 5; find whose names are used in the sacrament prayer.
Optional: read before the promise in segment 6 and ask when they have felt the Savior near in a group gathered in His name.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Chibota
aligned_quotes.text: Often, helping others feel seen as children of God begins with something as simple as learning their name.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Kyungu
aligned_quotes.text: Let us use the language that uplifts, edifies, comforts, and brings people together.

invitations.text: Please, come and see, come and help, and come and belong.
let us not miss the unifying power of the sacrament
I invite you to join the Christ-centered unity we are trying to build.

takeaways: The Savior reached out to people others shut out, and He invites all to come unto Him.
Unity does not come from agreeing on everything; it comes from each of us moving closer to Jesus Christ.
Small steps count: a name learned, a seat offered, a kind word in a chat.
act: Build the one bridge you wrote on your card before next Sunday.
Learn the name of one person at school or church you do not know yet, and use it the next time you see them.
When a conversation or group chat turns against someone, say one thing that brings people together, or message that person something kind.
During the sacrament on Sunday, look down your row and think: we are doing this together.
adapt: At home or with two or three youth: skip the race and read Luke 10:30–37 together; talk through one of the three situations and act it out as a family.
Large class: run the role plays in six groups, two for each situation, and watch only one for each.
Short on time: drop segment 5 and read the fourth key quote during segment 6.

children.title: Jesus Brings Us Together
children.big_idea: Jesus loves everyone and brings us together; when we come closer to Him, we come closer to each other.
children.objective: Children will say that Jesus brings us together and choose one way to help someone feel they belong this week.
prepare: Read President Uchtdorf’s talk, “Christ-Centered Unity.” You will teach one idea from it: Jesus brings us together.
Bring a picture of the Savior.
Bring a blanket or sheet and a soft ball.
Bring paper and crayons for each child.
Clear a space big enough for the children to stand in a wide circle.

segments.name: Welcome and one short truth
steps: Greet each child by name. Sing “Jesus Said Love Everyone” and invite a child to pray.

Teach the truth with actions: hold your hands far apart, then bring them together and clasp them while saying, Jesus brings us together. Have the children do it with you three times: once in a regular voice, once in a whisper, once standing up.
Tell them that President Uchtdorf, an Apostle of Jesus Christ, taught this at general conference.

segments.name: The blanket and the ball
steps: Lay the blanket flat on the floor with the ball in the middle. Ask one child to lift the blanket alone, holding just one corner, and keep the ball from rolling off. It will roll off. Thank the child for trying.
Now invite every child to hold an edge. Lift together and keep the ball in the middle. Try raising and lowering it slowly, then walking in a circle.
Sit down around the blanket. Ask the questions below.
Explain: Heavenly Father’s family is like this. Everyone is needed. President Uchtdorf said to each of us, “It would be incomplete without you.” Explain that incomplete means someone is missing.
questions: What happened when one person tried alone?

segments.name: Jesus loved people who were left out
steps: Hold up the picture of the Savior. Explain that when Jesus lived on the earth, many people stayed away from each other. Some would not talk to people from other places. President Uchtdorf taught that Jesus reached out to people who were left out.

Tell the story Jesus told in Luke 10:30–37 in simple words: a man was hurt and needed help. Two people saw him and walked by. Then a Samaritan came. People in that land usually stayed away from Samaritans, but he stopped, helped the man and took care of him.

Act it out. Choose a child to sit as the traveler who needs help, two to walk by, and one to be the Samaritan who stops, kneels and helps. Everyone else walks in place along the road. Repeat with new actors if time allows.
Ask the questions below. Then do the hand action and say the truth together again.
questions: Who was the kind one in the story?
Why do you think Jesus wants us to help people who are different from us?

segments.name: Step closer
steps: Put the picture of the Savior on a chair in the middle of the room. Have the children stand in a wide circle around it, arms stretched out so they cannot touch each other.

Explain that President Uchtdorf named ways to be more like Jesus: more patient, kinder, more forgiving, more helpful. Each time a child names something kind they can do, such as sharing, saying sorry, helping or waiting for a turn, everyone takes one step toward the picture.
Keep going until the children are shoulder to shoulder. Ask what happened to the space between them.
Read the first key quote slowly (“The closer we come to Him…”). Have the children repeat it after you in two parts.
questions: When we all came closer to Jesus, what happened to us?

segments.name: Draw a way to help someone belong
steps: Give each child paper and crayons. Share President Uchtdorf’s invitation: “Please, come and see, come and help, and come and belong.” Explain that to belong means to know you are wanted and needed.
Ask each child to draw themselves helping someone feel they belong: inviting someone to play, sitting by someone new, sharing, learning someone’s name.

As they draw, walk around and ask each child to tell you about the picture. Share President Chibota’s idea from this conference in your own words: helping someone feel seen can begin with learning their name.

segments.name: Show, promise and sing
steps: Invite each child to hold up their drawing and say in one sentence what they will do this week. This is your check for understanding.

Share President Uchtdorf’s promise in simple words: when we come together in Jesus’s name and build bridges and not walls, we will feel Heavenly Father close to us. Read the second key quote (“We have the Savior, and we have each other.”).
Bear a short testimony that each child is a child of God, as Elder Fale taught at this conference, and that Jesus loves every one of them.
Do the hand action and say the truth one last time. Sing “Love One Another” and close with prayer.
Follow up next week: ask who did what they drew. Let each child who wants to tell about it add a step toward the picture of the Savior.

key_quotes.text: The closer we come to Him, the closer we will come to each other
We have the Savior, and we have each other.
It would be incomplete without you.

scriptures.use: Tell the story in simple words in segment 3 and have the children act it out.
With older children, read it aloud in the last segment and ask where Jesus promises to be when we gather in His name.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Fale
aligned_quotes.text: I am a child of God and He loves me.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Chibota
aligned_quotes.text: Often, helping others feel seen as children of God begins with something as simple as learning their name.

invitations.text: Please, come and see, come and help, and come and belong.

takeaways: I can help someone feel they belong.
act: Do what you drew: help one person feel they belong this week.
Learn the name of one child at church or school you do not know yet.
At home, do the hand action and tell your family that Jesus brings us together.

adapt.younger: Ages 3–7: keep each part short and moving. Do the blanket and ball twice, tell the story in four sentences and let every child have a turn being the helper. In the stepping game, name the kind things yourself and let the children shout a step word together. Give a helper the job of holding the picture of the Savior. Repeat the hand action and the truth after every activity.
adapt.older: Ages 8–11: invite a child to read Luke 10:33–34 aloud before the acting, and another to read Matthew 18:20 at the end. Let an older child lead the stepping game. Ask a harder question: President Uchtdorf said baptism makes us part of a covenant people; how can someone who has been baptized help everyone at church feel they belong? Mention that at the sacrament we all remember Jesus together.
